questionText: Where is the ICAR-National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources (NBAGR)—the nodal national agency responsible for phenotypic/genetic characterization, registration, and Accession Number assignment of indigenous livestock and poultry breeds in India—located?
explanation: ICAR-NBAGR (established in 1984 at Bangalore and shifted to Karnal, Haryana in 1985) is the nodal agency that registers and assigns official Accession Numbers (format: INDIA_SPECIES_STATE_BREEDNAME_CODE) to sovereign indigenous livestock and poultry breeds of India.

questionText: In the official ICAR-NBAGR breed registration accession code format (for example, 'INDIA_CATTLE_0500_GIR_03005'), what do the four segments after 'INDIA' represent sequentially?
options: Donor Country -> Exotic Blood Level -> Generation Number -> Herd Book Volume
Breeding Institute -> Chromosome Count -> Heritability Class -> Year of Registration
Agro-Climatic Zone -> Milk Yield Rank -> Coat Color Code -> Conservation Threat Code
Species Name -> Native State Code -> Registered Breed Name -> Species/Breed Serial Code
explanation: Every NBAGR-registered indigenous breed receives a standardized alphanumeric Accession Number: INDIA_[SPECIES]_[STATE CODE]_[BREED NAME]_[SPECIES+BREED CODE], uniquely documenting its species, primary home-tract state, and breed serial number.

questionText: Which indigenous cattle breed of India—native to the Rann of Kutch and Banaskantha districts of Gujarat—is the HEAVIEST Indian cattle breed, renowned for its large lyre-shaped horns, pendulous sheath, and distinctive 'Sawai Chal' (1.25 pace) gait?
options: Punganur (dwarf cattle breed of Andhra Pradesh)
explanation: Kankrej (native to north Gujarat / Kutch) is the heaviest indigenous Bos indicus breed, prized as a powerful dual-purpose (milch and fast draft) animal characterized by massive lyre-shaped horns and the rhythmic 'Sawai Chal' gait.

questionText: Among the registered indigenous cattle breeds of India, which classification correctly groups the breeds into Milch breeds, Dual-purpose breeds, and Draft breeds?
options: Milch: Sahiwal, Gir, Red Sindhi, Rathi;  Dual-purpose: Tharparkar, Hariana, Kankrej, Ongole;  Draft: Hallikar, Amritmahal, Kangayam, Khillari
Milch: Hallikar, Kangayam, Nagori, Bargur;  Dual-purpose: Sahiwal, Gir, Red Sindhi;  Draft: Tharparkar, Kankrej, Ongole, Rathi
Milch: Vechur, Punganur, Ponwar, Kherigarh;  Dual-purpose: Kangayam, Hallikar;  Draft: Red Sindhi, Sahiwal, Gir, Deoni
Milch: Ongole, Khillari, Malvi, Siri;  Dual-purpose: Amritmahal, Pulikulam, Dangi;  Draft: Sahiwal, Gir, Rathi, Tharparkar
explanation: India's four premier Milch breeds are Sahiwal, Gir, Red Sindhi, and Rathi; major Dual-purpose breeds are Tharparkar, Hariana, Kankrej, Ongole, Mewati, and Deoni; and premier Draft breeds include Amritmahal, Hallikar, Kangayam, Khillari, Nagori, and Bargur.

questionText: Which indigenous riverine buffalo breed—native to the Chambal and Yamuna ravine tracts of Agra and Etawah (Uttar Pradesh) and Bhind/Morena (Madhya Pradesh)—is characterized by a copper-colored body coat, two white collar chevrons ('Kanthy') on the ventral neck, and the HIGHEST milk fat percentage (up to 12–13%)?
explanation: The Bhadawari buffalo of the Chambal/Yamuna ravines (UP and MP) has a characteristic copper-colored coat with pale legs and two white neck stripes ('Kanthy'), and is famous for producing milk with the highest butterfat content (8% average, reaching up to 12.5–13.0%).

questionText: Which of the following correctly pairs the distinctive horn morphology and home tract of the indigenous buffalo breeds 'Murrah', 'Surti', 'Jaffarabadi', and 'Pandharpuri'?
options: Murrah: sickle-shaped horns (Kerala); Surti: heavy drooping horns (Haryana); Jaffarabadi: lyre-shaped upright horns (Tamil Nadu); Pandharpuri: tightly curled horns (Gujarat)
Murrah: long sword-shaped horns (Maharashtra); Surti: tightly curled horns (Punjab); Jaffarabadi: sickle-shaped horns (Odisha); Pandharpuri: hornless polled skull (Assam)
Murrah: tightly curled Jalebi horns; Surti: flat sickle-shaped horns; Jaffarabadi: heavy drooping horns with sleepy eyes; Pandharpuri: very long sword-shaped horns up to 1.5 m
Murrah: upward lyre horns (Rajasthan); Surti: spiral corkscrew horns (Bihar); Jaffarabadi: short straight horns (Andhra Pradesh); Pandharpuri: drooping horns (Punjab)
explanation: Classic NBAGR morphological markers: Murrah (Haryana) has short, tightly curled spiral horns; Surti (Charotar tract, Gujarat) has medium flat sickle-shaped horns; Jaffarabadi (Gir, Gujarat) is the heaviest breed with massive frontal bones ('sleepy eyes') and drooping horns; Pandharpuri (Solapur/Kolhapur, Maharashtra) has extremely long, twisted sword-like horns reaching the back.

questionText: Among indigenous Indian sheep breeds, which breed is celebrated as the 'Merino of Rajasthan' (finest carpet/apparel wool), which is the tallest mutton breed of India, and which dwarf breed of West Bengal carries the prolific Booroola (FecB) gene?
options: Chokla ('Merino of Rajasthan'); Nellore (tallest sheep breed); Garole (prolific FecB carrier of Sundarbans)
Marwari ('Merino of Rajasthan'); Mandya (tallest sheep breed); Changthangi (prolific FecB carrier)
Malpura ('Merino of Rajasthan'); Garole (tallest sheep breed); Gaddi (prolific FecB carrier)
Sonadi ('Merino of Rajasthan'); Chokla (tallest sheep breed); Nellore (prolific FecB carrier)
explanation: Chokla (Shekhawati region of Rajasthan) yields the finest wool among Rajasthani sheep ('Merino of Rajasthan'); Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) is the tallest Indian sheep breed; and Garole (Sundarbans, West Bengal) is a micro-sheep carrying the FecB mutation with high twinning/triplets and resistance to foot-rot.

questionText: Which indigenous Indian goat breeds are respectively famous for: (i) being the tallest Indian goat breed with a prominent Roman nose and long pendulous ears (Etawah, UP), (ii) world-renowned glaze kid leather ('Morocco leather') and high twinning (West Bengal), and (iii) producing ultra-fine Pashmina (Cashmere) fiber in Ladakh?
explanation: Jamunapari (Chakarnagar, Etawah UP) is the tallest Indian goat with a convex Roman nose and long pendulous ears; Black Bengal (West Bengal) is a dwarf prolific breed yielding the world's finest shoe-upper leather; and Changthangi (along with Chegu in Ladakh/HP) produces warm Pashmina undercoat (11–14 microns).

questionText: The indigenous 'Kadaknath' (Kalamasi) poultry breed—native to Jhabua and Dhar districts of Madhya Pradesh and awarded a Geographical Indication (GI) tag—exhibits intense black-bluish pigmentation of its skin, shanks, bones, nerves, and internal organs due to:
options: Sex-linked dominant barring (B) combined with the White Leghorn dominant inhibitor (I) allele
Dermal fibromelanosis caused by a complex genomic duplication involving the Endothelin-3 (EDN3) gene
Homozygous recessive albinism at the tyrosinase (TYR) locus coupled with dietary iron overload
Chronic accumulation of biliverdin and hemosiderin resulting from hereditary hemolytic anemia
explanation: Kadaknath poultry exhibit 'fibromelanosis' (Fm)—an autosomal dominant dermal hyperpigmentation caused by an inverted duplication of the Endothelin-3 (EDN3) genomic region on chromosome 20, promoting massive proliferation and migration of melanin-producing melanoblasts throughout visceral connective tissues.

questionText: The unique 'Kharai' camel breed—registered by ICAR-NBAGR from the coastal Kachchh region of Gujarat—possesses which extraordinary ecological and physiological adaptation that distinguishes it from other dromedary camel breeds?
options: It possesses two dorsal humps and a thick woollen coat adapted to sub-zero Ladakh glaciers
It is a miniature hornless camel that subsists exclusively on subterranean desert tubers
It is an obligate carnivore cameloid hybrid bred for high-altitude polo in Manipur
It can swim in deep coastal seawater to graze on island mangrove trees (Avicennia marina)
explanation: The Kharai ('salty') camel of coastal Kutch (Gujarat) is a unique ecotope of dromedary camel that swims up to 3 km in Arabian Sea creek waters to browse on saline coastal mangroves (cher / Avicennia marina).

questionText: In the scientific conservation of threatened indigenous Animal Genetic Resources (AnGR), what is the exact operational distinction between 'In-situ conservation', 'Ex-situ in-vivo conservation', and 'Ex-situ in-vitro conservation'?
options: In-situ: live animals kept in their native habitat
In-situ: maintaining animals in foreign zoos only; Ex-situ in-vivo: keeping animals in native villages; Ex-situ in-vitro: rearing cloned calves on pasture
In-situ: crossbreeding scrub cows with exotic HF semen; Ex-situ in-vivo: culling all indigenous bulls; Ex-situ in-vitro: keeping stuffed museum specimens
In-situ: freezing embryos in liquid nitrogen; Ex-situ in-vivo: sequencing genomic DNA on microarrays; Ex-situ in-vitro: grazing animals in village commons
explanation: According to FAO and NBAGR definitions: In-situ conservation maintains live breeding herds within their original agro-ecological home tract and community production system; Ex-situ in-vivo maintains live animals outside their natural habitat (e.g., institutional farms/zoos outside the tract); and Ex-situ in-vitro (cryoconservation) stores frozen semen, oocytes, embryos, somatic cells, or DNA in liquid nitrogen at -196 C.
